title: Budgets & variances
examples: How do I know which variance to calculate first?
What is the difference between a flexible and a static budget?
Can variances tell me if I should change my prices?

explain.say: Today we are learning about budgets and variances in accounting.

items: Budgets help plan for the future.
We check if things went well or poorly.

explain.say: A flexible budget adjusts for changes in activity levels.

items: Recalculate costs based on the new level.

explain.say: For example, if you plan for fifty units but sell seventy, the budget changes.
A favourable variance means you spent less than expected costs.
An adverse variance means you spent more than the budget allowed. This is bad.
In real life, a shop uses variances to check its sales performance.

faq.q: What is the main difference between a static and flexible budget?
faq.a: A static budget is set for one activity level, while a flexible budget changes to match the actual activity level.
asks: Does the budget change if sales change?
How do I adjust the budget for different volumes?

faq.q: If I have a favourable variance, does that mean I made more profit?
faq.a: It means your costs were lower than expected for the actual output, which is good for profit.
asks: Is a favourable variance always good?
What does a favourable cost variance mean?

faq.q: When should I use a flexible budget in my business?
faq.a: You should use it whenever your actual output is likely to be different from your planned output.
asks: When is a flexible budget most useful?
Do I need a flexible budget for every report?

faq.q: How do I calculate the variance amount?
faq.a: You usually subtract the budgeted amount from the actual amount to find the difference.
asks: What is the formula for variance?
Do I multiply the difference by the units?

faq.q: Can I have both favourable and adverse variances at the same time?
faq.a: Yes, it is possible to have a favourable variance in materials but an adverse variance in labour.
asks: Is it normal to have mixed variances?

facts: A flexible budget adjusts budgeted costs for changes in activity levels.
A favourable variance means actual costs are less than budgeted costs.
An adverse variance means actual costs are more than budgeted costs.
The comparison of actual results to a budget is what creates a variance.

quiz.say: A factory planned to make 100 items at a cost of $500. If they actually make 150 items and the cost is $750, what is the variance?
quiz.why: The flexible budget suggests the cost for 150 units should be $750, which matches the actual cost, resulting in zero variance.

wrong.0: This assumes the actual cost was lower than the budgeted cost for 150 units.
wrong.1: This incorrectly compares the original budget of 100 units to the actual cost.
wrong.2: This only calculates the difference in units without adjusting the total cost.

quiz.say: If a company budgeted for 20 hours of labour but used 25 hours, and this is an adverse variance, what does this indicate?

options.show: They used more labour time than planned.
options.say: They used more labour time than planned.

quiz.why: An adverse variance in hours means the actual time spent exceeded the standard time allowed.

wrong.1: Efficiency is usually linked to the rate, not the total hours exceeding the budget.
wrong.2: Spending more time generally means higher labour costs.
wrong.3: While possible, the variance itself only states the difference, not the cause.

quiz.say: A manager compares actual sales of $15,000 against a flexible budget of $14,000 for the same volume. What is the variance?
quiz.why: Since actual sales are higher than the budget for that volume, the variance is favourable.

wrong.0: This incorrectly uses the actual figure as the variance amount.
wrong.2: This incorrectly assumes that higher sales always mean a negative variance.
wrong.3: A variance exists whenever actual results differ from the budget.
